data.hypothesis: The selected parent retains split source ranges, rsqrtf, and factor-eight unrolling. This experiment changes only the final velocity arithmetic: for target masses whose reciprocal remains in the normal finite range, compute one reciprocal and reuse it across the three force components; retain the original component-wise division outside that range. Reusing the reciprocal may reduce repeated divisions, but compiler common-subexpression handling and changed rounding could erase the benefit or affect correctness. No speedup is assumed before controller validation.

memory_lessons.applicability: For this kernel, loop-unroll factor results are non-monotonic in the recorded search measurements; isolate arithmetic changes against a fixed loop implementation rather than infer performance from unroll size alone.
memory_lessons.claim: The valid split-range/rsqrt factor-four candidate measured 0.000899482 s, compared with 0.001013465 s for factor eight and 0.000983105 s for factor two. These measurements do not establish why the factor-four program was faster.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure the reciprocal-reuse arithmetic change with the current factor-eight parent held fixed, then compare against the factor-four candidate if it validates.

data.notes: Only src/nbody_kernel.cu is changed. The self-interaction remains excluded by split ranges, and the existing interaction arithmetic and launch configuration are retained. The reciprocal path is guarded by a normal finite mass interval; other masses use the original component-wise division. This proposal has not been run or measured; controller correctness checks should include coincident positions, extreme mass, and FP64 tolerance before timing scored sizes.
transformations: Keep the one-target-per-thread mapping, split source ranges, rsqrtf interaction factor, factor-eight unrolling, and existing launch configuration unchanged.
Reuse one reciprocal of the target mass across the three velocity components only within a normal finite reciprocal-safe interval; use the original component-wise divisions outside that interval.
